title: Paper 2 Question 4: comparing viewpoints and perspectives
specPoints: Paper 2 Section A: Question 4 (AO3, 16 marks): comparing writers' perspectives and methods across both sources

tips.title: Both, in the first sentence
tips.body: Every paragraph opens with one idea and both writers' perspectives on it, with a difference. If a paragraph reaches the second writer only in its last line, it has compared for one sentence.

tips.title: Perspective and method, together
tips.body: AO3 is what each writer thinks and how it is conveyed. A method from each text in every paragraph, quoted and named, set against the corresponding choice in the other.

tips.title: The alternating answer
tips.body: A page on each source and a however at the end is some attempt at comparison, the Level 2 wording. Whereas, unlike, both … but, in every paragraph.

tips.title: Corresponding methods
tips.body: Exclamation against understatement; speech against reported reasoning; hyperbole against figures; a list that undercuts itself against a phrase that means every word. Find the pair and the comparison of methods writes itself.

tips.title: A perspective that moves
tips.body: The June 2024 example saw the doctor shift from horror to exhilaration and undercut himself with a casual Sure. A label is clear; a shape is perceptive.

tips.title: End on a verdict
tips.body: What each writer thinks the subject is: a vocation or a career; a calling or a calculation. The difference sharpened into what each text is for, and the period in a sentence where the text shows it.

why.matters: Two people write about the same thing and mean different things by it, and the reader who can say how, and how each writer's choices carry the difference, has the skill that reading any argument requires. Question 4 gives sixteen marks, the largest reading question on Paper 2 and the only test of AO3 in the qualification, for holding two texts together and comparing not just what each writer feels but how each makes a reader feel it. It is the reading skill behind every debate, every pair of reviews, every two accounts of the same event, and it is built from the habits the earlier questions taught: inference, method, effect, and now difference.

examples.title: Two sides of the same argument
examples.body: Two columnists on the same policy, two witnesses to the same accident, two reviews of the same play: the reader who can say that one persuades by figures and the other by a story, that one undercuts his own case with a joke and the other means every word, is doing Question 4. The comparison of methods is what lets a reader decide between them instead of being carried by whichever was read last.

examples.title: The account that asks to be felt and the one that asks to be judged
examples.body: Seacole wants the reader beside the pallet; Shackleton wants the reader inside the decision. Most writing that matters wants one or the other, and a reader who knows which is being asked, and by what choices, can give a writer their feeling or their assent on purpose. That is the difference between reading and being read to.

steps.title: Question 4: sixteen marks, both sources whole
steps.body:
Question 4 is the largest reading question on Paper 2 and the only question on either paper that assesses AO3: compare writers' ideas and perspectives, and how these are conveyed, across two texts. June 2024: for this question you need to refer to the whole of Source A together with the whole of Source B; compare how the writers convey their different feelings and perspectives on providing medical care. Three bullets: compare their feelings and perspectives; compare the methods they use to convey them; support with references to both texts.

**Four levels.** Level 4, 13 to 16, perceptive, detailed comparison: compares ideas and perspectives in a perceptive way; analyses how writers' methods are used; a range of judicious supporting detail from both texts; detailed and perceptive understanding of the different ideas and perspectives in both texts. Level 3, 9 to 12, clear, relevant comparison. Level 2, 5 to 8, some attempts at comparison. Level 1, 1 to 4, simple cross-reference.

**Two things are compared, always together.** What each writer thinks and feels about the subject, and how each conveys it. A paragraph that compares feelings without methods, or methods without feelings, is half a paragraph.

**Time.** About sixteen minutes, a mark a minute, at the end of Section A.

rows: Perceptive, detailed comparison; analyses methods; judicious detail from both texts
Clear, relevant comparison; explains methods clearly; relevant detail from both
Some attempts at comparison; some comment on methods

steps.title: Perspective and method: what the scheme listed
steps.body:
A perspective is the position a writer takes on the subject, the feelings and judgements that run through the text. A method is a choice that conveys it. The June 2024 indicative content lists both.

**Ideas the scheme named:** the writers' motivation; the nature of their work; their experiences of treating others; their training; their purpose.

**Methods the scheme named:** tone, Source A humorous, sarcastic, caustic, Source B emotive, serious, worthy; first person in both, and direct address in both for different purposes; speech in Source B to bring the scene to life; structural shifts in both, from training or arrival to actual practice; language features, metaphor, hyperbole and repetition in A, emotive language, rhetorical question and exclamation in B; and word choices.

**Read it as a plan.** One idea, motivation, say; each writer's perspective on it; the method each uses to convey that perspective, with a quotation; the difference stated. Three such paragraphs are sixteen marks.

steps.title: The Level 4 example, read as a shape
steps.body:
The June 2024 Level 4 indicative standard is worth reading for its moves rather than its content.

**It starts with a perspective that moves.** The doctor's perspective is described as constantly shifting, from the horror of night shifts to the exhilaration of surviving one. **It quotes a method and names it:** a list, “Sure it was hard work, sure the hours were bordering on inhumane”, with the adjective “inhumane” for the brutality of the work. **It reads a second choice against the first:** the casual “Sure” undercuts the suffering, and the proud “but I was a doctor now” makes it a badge of honour. **Then the other writer, on the same idea:** the nurse is entirely concerned with her patients and embraces her humble position; her awe is in “the sympathy and brotherly love shown by the strong to the weak”, with “brotherly” suggesting a family's self-sacrificing care. **And the difference, sharpened:** for Seacole medicine is a spiritual vocation; for the doctor, a professional prestige.

Perspective, method, method against method, the other writer, the difference. That is one paragraph of a sixteen-mark answer.

steps.title: The practice pair, compared
steps.body:
Seacole and Shackleton are both writing about deciding to act where help is short, and the comparison runs the way the scheme's list runs.

**Perspective.** Seacole's is that helping is a calling she cannot resist: she “waited for no permission” and ran to the wounded man at once. Shackleton's is that action is a leader's calculation: “That conclusion was forced upon me”, and the case for the journey “required to be argued in some detail”.

**Method against method.** Seacole conveys hers through emotive language and exclamation, “God help him!”, and through speech that brings the scene to life, the man's “God bless you, woman”; the reader is put beside the pallet. Shackleton conveys his through understatement and arithmetic, 540 miles, 800 miles, one month's provisions, so the reader is put inside the calculation.

**Structure.** Both move from arrival to practice: Seacole from the harbour to the wharf, Shackleton from the beach to the plan. **Person and address.** Both first person; Seacole prays aloud, Shackleton addresses the reader as someone owed an account.

**The difference, sharpened.** Both writers act without waiting to be asked, but Seacole writes to make the reader feel what she felt and Shackleton writes to make the reader agree that he was right.

steps.title: A Level 4 paragraph on the pair
steps.body: Focus: compare how the writers convey their different perspectives on the danger they face. Here is one paragraph to the descriptors.

visuals.problem: Write a Level 4 comparison paragraph on the danger each writer faces.

steps.text: The idea and both perspectives in one sentence: both writers face danger they did not have to face, but Seacole treats hers as beneath notice and Shackleton treats his as a thing to be measured.
steps.note: One idea, two perspectives, a difference: synthesis from the first line.

steps.text: Seacole's method: the danger to herself is never named; what she notices is the man, “groaning heavily”, and she breaks into prayer, “God help him!”, so the emotive language and the exclamation turn the reader's attention where hers is, away from her own risk.
steps.note: Method quoted, named, and read for its effect on the reader.

steps.text: Shackleton's method, against it: the danger is stated in a superlative, “the most tempestuous storm-swept area of water in the world”, then reduced to arithmetic, and the calm of the report makes the reader do the fearing; the understatement conveys a leader who has weighed the risk and will not dramatise it.
steps.note: The other writer's method, set against the first, with its own effect.

steps.text: A second method compared: Seacole gives the wounded man speech, so that the reader hears the danger through someone else; Shackleton gives the reader his own reasoning, so that the reader shares the decision rather than the fear.
steps.note: Two methods in one sentence: speech against reasoning.

steps.text: The difference, sharpened, with the period: an earnest Victorian memoir asks the reader to feel; an expedition leader's account, written after the war, asks the reader to judge that he was right.
steps.note: The perspectives explained by what each text is for, and when it was written.

steps.title: Comparing, not alternating
steps.body:
The commonest Question 4 answer describes Source A for a page and Source B for a page and adds *however, Source B is different*. It has compared for one sentence.

**One idea per paragraph, both texts in it.** Motivation; the nature of the work; the danger; the people around them. Each paragraph takes one and puts both writers to it.

**The difference in the grammar.** *Whereas*, *unlike*, *both … but*, *where Seacole …, Shackleton …*. If a paragraph has no comparative connective, it is not comparing.

**Methods compared as methods.** Exclamation against understatement; speech against reasoning; hyperbole against figures. A method named in one text calls for the corresponding choice in the other.

**The period explains, when it does.** Sixty or a hundred and sixty years between the sources is why the perspectives differ, sometimes: a Victorian memoir's piety, a diary's modern irony. Say it when the text shows it, in a sentence, not as a paragraph of history.

steps.title: Plan a Question 4 answer in three lines
steps.body:
Focus: compare how the two writers convey their different perspectives on the people they are trying to help.

Write three lines, one per paragraph, each with: the idea; both perspectives with a difference; one method from each text with a quotation.

1. Who the people are to each writer: the wounded man and the men on the beach.
2. What each writer does with speech: the artilleryman's words, and the volunteers Shackleton reports.
3. What each text asks the reader to feel about those people.

Then write the second paragraph in full, in five minutes.

steps.title: Perceptive: perspective as a shape, difference as a verdict
steps.body:
The Level 4 words are perceptive comparison, analysis of methods, judicious detail from both, and detailed understanding of the different ideas. Four habits produce them.

**Read a perspective as a shape.** The June 2024 example saw the doctor's perspective shifting between horror and exhilaration and being undercut by his own tone. A perspective that moves, or that the writer's method complicates, is perceptive; a label, proud or humble, is clear.

**Compare methods that correspond.** Exclamation in one against understatement in the other; speech against reported reasoning; hyperbole against figures. The comparison of methods is where AO3 differs from two Question 3 answers side by side.

**Judicious from both.** Short quotations, chosen because each carries a perspective, from both texts in every paragraph.

**End on a verdict.** What each writer thinks the subject is: a vocation or a career; a calling or a calculation. The difference sharpened into what each text is for.

**Sixteen minutes, three paragraphs,** and then the writing task.

steps.title: Question 4 in one page
steps.body:
Sixteen marks, sixteen minutes, both sources whole, AO3.

- **Two things compared together:** feelings and perspectives, and the methods that convey them, with references to both texts.
- **The scheme's list:** ideas such as motivation, the nature of the work, treating others, training, purpose; methods such as tone, person and address, speech, structural shifts, language features, word choices.
- **The shape:** one idea per paragraph; both perspectives in the first sentence with a difference; a method from each, set against the other; the difference sharpened.
- **Comparing, not alternating:** whereas, unlike, both … but, in every paragraph.
- **Perceptive:** a perspective that moves or is undercut; corresponding methods; a verdict on what each writer thinks the subject is.

Practised on Seacole's calling and Shackleton's calculation.

questions.prompt: Compare how the writers convey their different perspectives on helping others. Refer to the whole of the Seacole passage and the whole of the Shackleton passage. Write a full Question 4 answer of about the length you would write for sixteen marks: three paragraphs, each with both perspectives, a method from each text set against the other, and a difference sharpened.
questions.solution:
Both writers help where no one has asked them to, but Seacole writes helping as an impulse she cannot resist and Shackleton writes it as a responsibility he has to reason his way to. Seacole conveys the impulse through the speed of her own sentences: she “waited for no permission”, she ran to the man at once, and the exclamation “God help him!” breaks her description as if the feeling could not wait for the grammar. Shackleton conveys responsibility through the slowness of his: “That conclusion was forced upon me”, and the case “required to be argued in some detail”, so that the reader is made to walk through the reasoning at the pace he did. Where her method is emotive language and exclamation, his is understatement and figures, and the difference in method is the difference in perspective: she feels first, he decides first.

Both let other people into the account, but for opposite purposes. Seacole gives the wounded man his own voice, “God bless you, woman”, repeated, so that the reader hears her worth from a patient rather than from her, and the speech brings the wharf to life in the way the June 2024 scheme found speech doing in her text. Shackleton reports his men's wish to volunteer in his own summary, so that the reader hears their loyalty through the leader who has to weigh it and refuse some of it. One writer lets the reader be told; the other tells.

Both accounts move from arrival to action, and both are first person, but they ask different things of the reader. Seacole's earnest Victorian memoir asks to be felt with: the poor fellow, the prayer, the woman's hand on a wharf full of men. Shackleton's account, written after a war that had made understatement the register of courage, asks to be judged and agreed with: the most tempestuous sea in the world stated once and left, the arithmetic of miles and provisions. For Seacole helping is a calling that leaves no room for her own danger; for Shackleton it is a calculation that leaves no room for feeling, and the reader who finishes both knows which writer wanted their heart and which wanted their assent.

questions.modelAnswer:
Both writers help where no one has asked them to, but Seacole writes helping as an impulse she cannot resist and Shackleton writes it as a responsibility he has to reason his way to. Seacole conveys the impulse through the speed of her own sentences: she “waited for no permission”, she ran to the man at once, and the exclamation “God help him!” breaks her description as if the feeling could not wait for the grammar. Shackleton conveys responsibility through the slowness of his: “That conclusion was forced upon me”, and the case “required to be argued in some detail”, so that the reader is made to walk through the reasoning at the pace he did. Where her method is emotive language and exclamation, his is understatement and figures, and the difference in method is the difference in perspective: she feels first, he decides first.

Both let other people into the account, but for opposite purposes. Seacole gives the wounded man his own voice, “God bless you, woman”, repeated, so that the reader hears her worth from a patient rather than from her, and the speech brings the wharf to life in the way the June 2024 scheme found speech doing in her text. questions.prompt: Write one paragraph comparing the methods, not the feelings, by which the doctor of the June 2024 Source A and Mary Seacole convey their perspectives on their work, using the methods and quotations the mark scheme names: the doctor's list and casual Sure, and Seacole's brotherly love. Name each method, set them against each other, and say what each does to the reader.
questions.solution: The doctor conveys his perspective through a list that undercuts itself, and Seacole through a single phrase that will not: the two methods are opposites and convey opposite views of the same work. His list, “Sure it was hard work, sure the hours were bordering on inhumane”, piles up the brutality with the adjective “inhumane”, and then the casual “Sure” at the head of each clause waves it away, so that the reader hears a man who has learned to tolerate suffering and, with “but I was a doctor now”, to wear it as a badge; the effect is a perspective that mocks its own pride even as it asserts it. Seacole's method is the reverse of undercutting: “the sympathy and brotherly love shown by the strong to the weak” is stated without irony, and the word “brotherly” makes the doctors' care a family's, so that the reader is asked to admire what she admires without a joke to hide behind. Set against each other, a list that cancels itself and a phrase that means every word, the methods convey the difference the scheme names: for him medicine is a profession whose costs are survived, for her a vocation whose costs are a privilege.

questions.prompt: A student's Question 4 answer compares the two writers' feelings perceptively but never names a method or quotes either text. What is the ceiling?
questions.solution: AO3 is ideas and perspectives and how they are conveyed. An answer with the first half only cannot meet the descriptors for analysing methods or selecting judicious detail from both texts, however perceptive its account of the feelings.

markScheme.description: Well below Level 4: the descriptor asks for analysis of methods and judicious detail from both texts, and the answer has neither

Nothing, because Question 4 answers must begin with a method

questions.prompt: A student says: 'The two sources are from different centuries, so I should spend a paragraph on the history of each period.' What is the better account?
questions.solution: AO3 rewards comparison of perspectives and methods, and the period is useful when it explains why they differ. A sentence tied to a choice in the text does that; a paragraph of dates does not.

options: The period is irrelevant, and the two sources should be treated as if written in the same year
The period earns a sentence where the text shows it explaining a perspective; a paragraph of history compares nothing

examTechnique.body:
**Sixteen marks, sixteen minutes, both sources whole.** The only AO3 question on the paper.

**Two things compared, together.** Perspectives and the methods that convey them, with references to both texts in every paragraph.

**Three paragraphs, one idea each.** Both writers in the first sentence with a difference; a method from each, quoted and named, set against its counterpart; the difference sharpened.

**Comparing, not alternating.** Whereas, unlike, both … but. A page on each source with a however at the end is Level 2.

**Perceptive.** A perspective that moves or is undercut by the writer's own method; corresponding methods; a verdict on what each writer thinks the subject is. The period in a sentence where the text shows it.
examinerErrors: Describing each source in turn and comparing in one sentence at the end.
Comparing feelings without methods, or listing methods without the perspectives they convey.
Quoting from one source only, when the descriptor asks for judicious detail from both.
Labelling a perspective, proud or humble, rather than reading it as a shape.
Spending a paragraph on the history of each period instead of a sentence where the text shows it.
Running out of time, since Question 4 comes last in Section A and the writing task follows.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer holds both writers from its first sentence and never lets one go: each paragraph takes one idea, states both perspectives with a difference, quotes a method from each text, sets the two methods against each other as corresponding choices, and says what the difference conveys. It reads each perspective as a shape, noticing where a writer's own tone complicates his position, and it ends on a verdict about what each writer thinks the subject is, with the period in a sentence where the texts show it. Sixteen minutes, three paragraphs, both texts in every one.
